content: Loratadine is a medication prescribed to temporarily alleviate symptoms of hay fever, which is an allergic reaction to airborne substances such as pollen or dust, as well as other allergies. These symptoms include sneezing, a runny nose, and itching of the eyes, nose, or throat. It is also used to treat itching and redness caused by hives. However, loratadine does not prevent hives or other allergic skin reactions. Loratadine belongs to a class of medications known as antihistamines. It works by blocking the action of histamine, a substance in the body that triggers allergic symptoms. Loratadine is also available in combination with pseudoephedrine, but this information pertains only to loratadine used alone. If you are taking a combination product, consult the package label or your doctor for additional details. Loratadine is available in various forms, including syrup, tablets, and rapidly disintegrating tablets, all of which are taken orally. It is typically taken once daily, with or without food. Follow the instructions on the package label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take loratadine exactly as directed, and do not take more or less than recommended. Exceeding the recommended dose may cause drowsiness. If you are using the rapidly disintegrating tablet, carefully remove it from the blister package without breaking it. Do not push the tablet through the foil. Once removed, place the tablet on your tongue, close your mouth, and allow it to dissolve quickly. It can be swallowed with or without water. Do not use loratadine to treat hives that are bruised, blistered, unusually colored, or do not itch. Contact your doctor if you experience this type of hives. Stop taking loratadine and consult your doctor if your hives do not improve within the first three days of treatment or if they persist for more than six weeks. If the cause of your hives is unknown, contact your doctor. If you develop symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing; swelling in or around the mouth or tongue; wheezing; drooling; dizziness; or loss of consciousness, seek emergency medical attention immediately. These may be signs of a life-threatening allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. If your doctor suspects you are at risk for anaphylaxis, they may prescribe an epinephrine injector (e.g., EpiPen). Do not use loratadine as a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use loratadine if the safety seal is broken or missing. Loratadine may be recommended for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking loratadine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to loratadine, any other medications, or any ingredients in the loratadine product you will be using. Check the package label for a list of ingredients. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take, especially medications for colds and allergies. Notify your doctor if you have or have ever had asthma, kidney disease, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking loratadine, contact your doctor. If you have phenylketonuria (PKU), be aware that some brands of orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking loratadine. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Loratadine may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: headache, dry mouth, nosebleed, sore throat, mouth sores, difficulty falling or staying asleep, nervousness, weakness, stomach pain, diarrhea, or red or itchy eyes. Some side effects may be serious. Stop taking loratadine and contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: rash, hives, itching, swelling of the eyes, face, lips, tongue, throat, hands, arms, feet, ankles, or lower legs; hoarseness; difficulty breathing or swallowing; or wheezing. Store loratadine in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat, moisture, and light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Use orally disintegrating tablets immediately after removing them from the blister package and within six months of opening the outer foil pouch. Write the date of opening on the product label to track the six-month period. Dispose of any expired or unused medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include a fast or pounding heartbeat, drowsiness, headache, or unusual body movements. Keep all appointments with your doctor, and consult your pharmacist if you have any questions about loratadine.
